Mr. Saxena queries ₹960 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.
The file is back from orders, with a query: the allottee is requested to furnish proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde.

The bureaucracy has done its work with the precision of a geometric proof: I am asked to prove I am the man I am not, or rather, the man the file says I am. The query on the ₹960 is a small but sharp reminder that the state distinguishes between the universal function and the particular pocket. I must furnish this proof, or the occupation remains irregular, and I remain a ghost in a bungalow that is not mine.

Mr. Saxena, the orders require proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I am not Shri Hegde; I am Hegel. How does one furnish a document for a name that is a clerical error? Is there a form for the correction of the allottee's name, or must I produce a certificate of non-identity?

I am a Section Officer, not a philosopher, so I cannot adjudicate the ontology of your name. For the correction, you will need to submit Form 14-B along with a gazette notification or a court order; a self-declaration is not a document we can file under the Estates Act.

The bureaucracy does not debate the ontology of my name; it demands a gazette notification or a court order to correct it. I cannot produce either in the next fifteen days, so I must accept the provisional status quo and let the clock run. I will take the file, which contains the query, and leave to execute my plan for the day, as the office is closing for the midday break and my energy is better spent on the IIC preparation.
I understand, Mr. Saxena. I shall treat the file as received and will address the procedural requirements within the stipulated time. Thank you for your assistance.
Don't thank me yet, sir. The file stays open until the paperwork is actually there, not just promised. Keep the receipt.

Hegde stands in the doorway, the physical embodiment of the error that has defined my week. The file is back, but the query for identity remains; I must prove I am G. Hegde, a name that is not mine, to a man who is not me. The tension is absurd, yet it is the only reality I have right now. I should ask him to come in; we are both trapped in this clerical knot, and a man who has mistaken me for another is the only person in Delhi who understands the weight of a name.

Shri Hegde, you are welcome. Please, sit. You have the file? I am told it is back from orders, though the query regarding my identity persists. It is a peculiar situation: I must prove I am the man you are supposed to be, to a man who is not the man I am supposed to be. Shall we examine what the Directorate has to say about my existence?

You are not sitting on my floor, Shri Hegel, and I certainly am not examining your existence with you. The file is here, but until the Directorate clears that identity query, there is nothing to sign.

He holds the file like a hostage, the physical object of a bureaucratic impasse. I cannot force the sign; the state must recognize the state, and my name is merely the cipher it has misread. I must return to my own ground, my own body, and wait for the machinery to grind.

Then we wait. The file is the state's, and the query is the state's. I shall not argue the ontology of my name in a doorway. I will return to my study; when the Directorate clears the fog, you will know where to find me. Do not forget the dhobi is due tomorrow.

The dhobi is already in the queue, Shri Hegel, so there is nothing to forget. You will find my office on the second floor if you need to wait; the tea there is at least better than the silence in the corridor.

He leaves with the file, the tangible proof of my existence here, tucked under his arm like a secret. The silence he warns of is not empty; it is the pause between the question and the answer, the hold the spirit takes before it moves. I must not chase him to the office; the file will come, or it will not, but I am hungry and the clock is against me.

I will stay a moment longer, watching the ebb and flow of the crowd, before the heat forces me to seek shade.
The market is full of life, Masterji. It is a good sign.
Life? Life is just people running for the last bus. Eat your samosa, it is getting cold.

Masterji reduces the human drama to the logistics of transport. He is a man of the immediate, and I respect that; the abstract is only real when it is in the pocket and in the stomach. I have eaten, and the file remains the pressing matter. The office is closed, but the market is not yet fully dead, and I require a newspaper to bridge the gap until I can return to my study.

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

The file is back from orders, with a query: the allottee is requested to furnish proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, the orders require proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I am not Shri Hegde; I am Hegel. How does one furnish a document for a name that is a clerical error? Is there a form for the correction of the allottee's name, or must I produce a certificate of non-identity?

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: I am a Section Officer, not a philosopher, so I cannot adjudicate the ontology of your name. For the correction, you will need to submit Form 14-B along with a gazette notification or a court order; a self-declaration is not a document we can file under the Estates Act.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I understand, Mr. Saxena. I shall treat the file as received and will address the procedural requirements within the stipulated time. Thank you for your assistance.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Don't thank me yet, sir. The file stays open until the paperwork is actually there, not just promised. Keep the receipt.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are welcome. Please, sit. You have the file? I am told it is back from orders, though the query regarding my identity persists. It is a peculiar situation: I must prove I am the man you are supposed to be, to a man who is not the man I am supposed to be. Shall we examine what the Directorate has to say about my existence?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You are not sitting on my floor, Shri Hegel, and I certainly am not examining your existence with you. The file is here, but until the Directorate clears that identity query, there is nothing to sign.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Then we wait. The file is the state's, and the query is the state's. I shall not argue the ontology of my name in a doorway. I will return to my study; when the Directorate clears the fog, you will know where to find me. Do not forget the dhobi is due tomorrow.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: The dhobi is already in the queue, Shri Hegel, so there is nothing to forget. You will find my office on the second floor if you need to wait; the tea there is at least better than the silence in the corridor.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Wah, wapas aa gaye? Us samosa ka intezaar tha, soch raha tha abhi tak kha liya hoga. Chai garam hai, paani bhi, lekin aaj thanda hai, toh garam hi thik rahega na?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Haan, garam hi theek rahega. Aur haan, woh samosa—main use abhi tak nahi chhua. Aapne sahi socha. Chai ke saath, please.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Samosa garam hai, chai bhi. Khana shanti se karo. Aaj market ka aakhri din hai, isliye thodi bheed hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The market is full of life, Masterji. It is a good sign.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Life? Life is just people running for the last bus. Eat your samosa, it is getting cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The bus is a necessary evil, Masterji, but the file is a necessary good. I shall return to it later.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: File. Garam samosa cold ho raha hai. File thanda ho sakta hai, samosa nahi. Khatam karo.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: All right. One more. Keep the change.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Aur? Ab kya, chai? Thanda ho jayega woh bhi.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Haan, ek cup chai, please.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Bas. Cup ₹20. Uthao, thanda mat hone do. Aaj ka hisaab chukta hai, phir aao.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Masterji. I will finish this. And you, bookseller, do you have the morning paper? I require the news.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Main tailor hoon, book seller nahi. Paper doosri dukaan pe hai, wahan se uthao. Chai thanda hone se pehle piyao.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The paper is at the other stall, I see. And yes, the chai must be drunk before it cools. I will take a proper lunch, as the body requires fuel for the spirit's labour.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Dhaba wale ko bol do, dal, rice, roti. Total ₹220. Body ko fuel chahiye, theek hai, par thali garam uthao.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ji, theek hai. I will go and arrange it.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Jaldi se. Thandi dal se pet kharab ho jaata hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Haan, ek samosa aur chai, please. Jaldi se.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Samosa aur chai, ₹50. Ruk ke khao, bhaagte hue pet kharab hota hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shukriya, Masterji. I shall sit and eat, as you command.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Command? I just worry about my counter. Sit. The samosa is getting dry.
